name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation containing photos of 91 object types in complex everyday scenes. The dataset contains 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images with per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick, 'Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context,' in ECCV, 2014.
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using queries for pairs of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs to gather non-iconic images containing contextual relationships and non-canonical object views. Images were harvested using searchable metadata and keywords, with at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Images were retrieved using pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using detection methods, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An explicit filtering stage was performed to remove iconic images when enough images could not be found through pairwise category searches. Workers were asked to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates using an AMT filtering task.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary tasks: (1) Category labeling using a hierarchical approach where workers indicated which object categories were present by dragging category icons onto instances; (2) Instance spotting where workers placed crosses on all instances of each category (up to 10 instances); (3) Instance segmentation where workers segmented each object instance using a modified interface from the OpenSurfaces project. For images with more than 10 instances of a category, crowd labeling was used where workers painted all pixels belonging to the category. Each image was labeled by 8 workers for category labeling and instance spotting stages.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Modified user interface from OpenSurfaces project for segmentation tasks.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were used for category labeling and instance spotting, with a category considered present if any worker indicated it. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators; if any indicated it was bad, it was shown to 2 additional workers. Segmentations that didn't receive at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded. Workers who consistently produced poor segmentations had all their work discarded.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers for category labeling and instance spotting stages. 1 worker for initial segmentation. 3-5 workers for segmentation verification.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two roughly equal parts. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release will contain a total of 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories (11 categories omitted). Some omitted categories may be added in the cumulative 2015 release.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was designed to address biases toward iconic views of objects. Previous datasets tended to contain images with single large objects in canonical perspectives centered in the image. MS COCO focuses on non-iconic images with objects in natural contexts, partially occluded, amid clutter, reflecting the composition of actual everyday scenes.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset only includes 'thing' categories (objects for which individual instances may be easily labeled) and not 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The dataset is limited to entry-level categories commonly used by humans when describing objects, excluding fine-grained categories and object-part categories. For images containing more than 10-15 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment; these areas are ignored during evaluation.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for three core research problems in scene understanding: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization of objects. Primary uses include object detection, instance segmentation, and training models capable of recognizing objects in their natural context. The dataset provides baseline performance analysis for bounding box and segmentation detection results. Training and validation data are released for model development; test data is available through an evaluation server.
